title: Ashtpadi 8, salok: the one who knows God
hookLine: the salok introduces the God-conscious one

lines: A SCRIPTURE THAT PAINTS A PERSON.
cards: Some passages of scripture are portraits. Not commands, not stories, but a description of a person: how they walk, how they speak, how they treat a stranger. Portraits work differently from rules.
You don't obey a portrait. You look at it, and something in you leans toward it. Ashtpadi seven described the holy company.
Ashtpadi eight zooms in on one face in that company and gives it a name. For eight stanzas, Guru Arjan paints the brahm giaanee.

teach.h: BRAHM: GOD. GIAANEE: ONE WHO KNOWS.
teach.b: Brahm giaanee. Brahm here is the Supreme, God beyond all forms. Giaan is knowing; giaanee is the one who knows.
So, the one who knows God. It's often put in English as the God-conscious one, and that's closer, because this knowing isn't information. It's not someone who has read the most books about God.
It's someone whose whole awareness is soaked in God, the way a cloth is soaked in dye. The salok gives three marks.

teach.h: TRUE IN MIND, TRUE IN MOUTH.
teach.b: True in the mind. True in the mouth, so what they say matches what they are, with no gap between inside and outside.

And they see nothing but the One: not that they stop seeing people or trees or traffic, but that in everything they see, they see the One. The salok ends: Nanak, these are the marks of the brahm giaanee.
The word for marks is lachhan, the features that make a face recognizable. That's the key.
The salok isn't handing out a title. You'd recognize such a person by these marks, not by robes or rank. Over the next stanzas the portrait fills in: a lotus, the earth, the sun, the wind.
Today, just look at the face, and notice that every mark is something you'd see in how a person lives.

how: Sikhs read ashtpadi eight of Sukhmani Sahib as a portrait of the brahm giaanee, drawn in marks and pictures rather than rules.

o: a scholar who has read every holy book
one whose whole awareness is soaked in God
a title given to the head of a temple

games.q: the eighth salok — tap the pairs.
p: no gap between inside and outside

s: a brahm giaanee is whoever has read the most about God
this knowing isn't information; it's an awareness soaked in God.
the salok gives marks you'd recognize, not a title
the salok says the brahm giaanee sees nothing but the One
in everything they see, they see the One.

games.q: someone introduces themselves as a brahm giaanee. by the salok, how would you know?
o: by the marks: true in mind and speech, seeing the One in all.
by how many followers they have.
games.why: Nanak, these are the marks of the brahm giaanee: the salok describes features, not a rank.

practice: Bring to mind someone wise and gentle you've actually met, not necessarily well-known, and notice how little gap there is between what they say and who they are, and how they look at a waiter, a child, a stranger.
You don't need to call them a saint; just let yourself lean toward what you see. If you pray, you can give thanks that such people exist.

wordCard.voice: Brahm giaanee. The one who knows God, the God-conscious one: true in mind, true in speech, seeing the One in all.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: brahm giaanee, the one who knows God; the portrait of ashtpadi eight.

carryVoice: Your line: the god-conscious one. Known by marks, not by robes or rank. That's day four hundred sixty-six.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)
